To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a method to determine the shape and location of attracting sets for a multistep method that is consistent, strictly stable and convergent, and that the method is applicable to dynamical systems with a non-unique asymptotically stable attracting set.

we establish an estimate for the change of a Lyapunova function on a discrete trajectory of a consistent, stable multistep approximation to a dynamical system, and we use this estimate to determine nearby attracting set and attractor for the discretized dynamical system, as done previously in Kloeden and Lörenz [3] for 1 step methods.

(a) for a consistent, strictly A-stable multistep method, the Lyapunov exponent of the discretized system on the attracting set of the continuous dynamical system is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number, and (b) for a consistent multistep method with a positive region of stability, the discretized system has a compact attracting set that is contained in a ball of radius that is bounded by a positive number.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problem: Let be a continuous dynamical system on an open set with an asymptoticaly stable attractor.
the question: how can we find the attracting set for a dynamical system approximated by a multistep method?

the question of whether the attractor of a dynamical system can be approximated by the attracting sets of a consistent, stable discretization of the dynamical system, i.e. the attracting sets of the discrete dynamical system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the attractors of the discretized system are contained in the attracting sets, which are defined by the uniform estimates of the Lyapunov functions.
multistep methods are not only a good choice for solving stiff ODEs but also for the numerical analysis of dynamical systems.
multistep methods are as good as 1-step methods for determining the attracting set of a dynamical system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the attracting sets of the discrete system are contained in a neighborhood of the attracting sets of continuous system.

, for a consistent and strictly stable multisteph method approximating the dynamics of an autonomous ODE, the discrete dynamical system generated by the method has nearby attracting sets and attracting sets of the same shape as the continuous system.
we can extend results for 1-step method to multistep methods, and the extension can be used to determine attractors of multistep methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the results of Kloeden and Lorenza can be extended to multistep methods.
, in contrast to 1-step methods, the multistep methods can be shown to have a unique attracting set and a unique attractor for a large range of step sizes.

multistep methods, which are often preferred over 1-step methods in practice for their stability properties, do not suffer any loss in the ability to approximate the attractors and attractor basins of the dynamical system.
